newsitem.title: USA: US EPA sets fuel-neutral standard for new boilers.
newsitem.headline: US EPA sets fuel-neutral standard for new boilers.

text.p: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency signed off on a rule setting a fuel-neutral emissions standard for new utility and industrial boilers, an EPA air and radiation office spokeswoman said Wednesday.

EPA expected the rule to affect about 17 utility boilers and 381 industry boilers likely to be built over the next five years, and reduce emissions of nitrogen oxides, which contribute to smog, by a total of about 46,000 tons a year.
Natural gas producers considered the new rule a major victory over the coal industry, which secured favorable treatment for existing boilers under the Clean Air Act.
"They've lost an unnatural advantage," said Bruce Craig, the Natural Gas Supply Association's environmental director.

Under the clean air law, emissions limits for existing boilers were set based on the fuel burned, which meant that higher polluting coal-fired boilers were allowed to meet less stringent emissions standards than natural gas-fired boilers.
Under the new rule, new boilers will have to meet emissions limits for nitrogen oxides (NOx) based on the amount of power produced by the facility, not based on the fuel used.
The rule applies in areas of the country that meet current smog limits.

"It's unnecessarily biased against coal," said Buddy Eller, a spokesman for Southern Co, one of the nation's biggest utility owners, which relies heavily on coal. "It basically eliminates coal as an option."
"The good news is that it doesn't apply retroactively to existing facilities," he said.

NGSA's Craig said coal-fired plants would be able to meet the new standard, but added that it made natural gas, which is more expensive than coal, a more economic choice because of its "low polluting and high efficiency qualities."
EPA had been sued by environmental groups to issue the new standards and was under a court-ordered deadline to complete them by July 1.
